PAPER: RESEARCH ARTICLE Published Online: December 10, 2025 https://doi.org/10.31893/multiscience.2026417 Strategic decision-making as a behavioral bridge: Mediating the impact of contingency factors on management accounting practices in digital start- ups Rasmi Nur Anggraenia | Andi Mattulada Amirb | Jurana Jurnanab | Rajindra Rajindraa aFaculty of Economics and Business, Universitas Muhammadiyah Palu, Palu, Indonesia. bFaculty of Economics and Business, Universitas Tadulako, Palu, Indonesia. Abstract This study investigates how strategic decision-making mediates the influence of operational technology, environmental uncertainty, organizational culture, and managerial knowledge on the adoption of Management Accounting Practices (MAPs) among digital start-ups in Palu, Indonesia. Drawing on contingency theory, this study emphasizes how behavioral mechanisms within managerial cognition translate contextual contingencies into accounting actions. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire distributed to seventy-two founders and financial managers of digital start-ups operating within the Palu metropolitan area. The analytical framework employed Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), using a bootstrapping technique with 5,000 resamples to assess reliability, convergent, and discriminant validity (CR, AVE, HTMT). The results indicate that organizational culture (β = 0.31, p < 0.01) and managerial knowledge (β = 0.37, p < 0.001) are the strongest predictors of strategic decision-making, which subsequently exerts a significant influence on the adoption of MAPs (β = 0.42, p < 0.001). Mediation analysis confirmed that strategic decision- making partially mediates the effects of culture and managerial knowledge on MAP adoption, while the impact of operational technology and environmental uncertainty remained indirect and limited. The model explains 46% of the variance in SDM and 52% in MAP adoption, reflecting robust predictive relevance (Q² > 0). These findings extend contingency theory by incorporating behavioral mediation, highlighting that effective strategic decision-making enables digital start-ups to adapt accounting practices in uncertain technological and environmental contexts. Practical implications include the need for incubator programs and policymakers to strengthen decision-making competencies and managerial cognition as integral parts of digital entrepreneurship training. Keywords: managerial cognition, contingency theory, entrepreneurial ventures, organizational culture, PLS-SEM, Indonesia 1. Introduction Digital start-ups in emerging markets are often confronted with critical barriers stemming from limited financial resources and unpredictable market conditions. These challenges hinder strategic and financial decision-making processes that are fundamental to the survival, scalability, and competitiveness of new ventures. Restricted access to external capital—largely driven by investor skepticism and perceived entrepreneurial risk—further exacerbates these limitations, weakening firms’ ability to manage risk and pursue sustainable growth (Carraro et al., 2020; Panda et al., 2021). In response, management accounting practices (MAPs) have gained prominence as essential managerial tools that enhance decision-making and organizational control. MAPs provide structured financial data and analytical insights, empowering start-ups to manage resources efficiently, align operational execution with strategic objectives, and respond proactively to dynamic environments. Empirical studies have consistently demonstrated that MAP implementation improves performance by promoting cost control, facilitating risk assessment, and strengthening strategic planning (Nugrahani et al., 2023; Reyroso et al., 2023; Zafar et al., 2024). Strategic management accounting (SMA) practices, in particular, offer forward- looking, value-oriented approaches that support adaptation and innovation in uncertain markets (Adeniran & Obembe, 2020; Andayani et al., 2024). To explain the organizational variation in MAP adoption, contingency theory remains a foundational framework. This theory posits that the efficacy of accounting systems is contingent upon the degree of alignment between internal practices and external contextual variables. Core contingencies—including operational technology, environmental uncertainty, organizational culture, and managerial knowledge—are believed to shape the adoption and effectiveness of accounting tools Multidiscip. The evidence indicates that firms exposed to volatile market environments adapt their accounting systems to mitigate external risk, thereby reinforcing the theory’s predictive value (Sumkaew & Intanon, 2020; Tran, 2023). Within digital start-ups, the need for agility and responsiveness in early development stages renders strategic decision- making especially pivotal. Founders must balance immediate operational demands with long-term strategic goals—a task that benefits significantly from timely, reliable accounting information. Through the implementation of MAPs, start-ups are better equipped to identify market opportunities, manage financial flows, and align capabilities with evolving strategies (Phornlaphatrachakorn & Kalasindhu, 2020; Uyar, 2019). Furthermore, SMA practices contribute to both internal control and external competitiveness by offering strategic insights into market positioning and value creation (Nanediri et al., 2022; Ojra et al., 2021; Remali et al., 2020). The positive correlation between MAP adoption and start-up performance is well documented. Firms employing structured MAPs report enhanced financial transparency, improved cost efficiency, and greater strategic responsiveness— attributes that are particularly vital during the vulnerable early phases of business development (Cleary et al., 2022; Nugraheni & Martono, 2023). These findings underscore the critical role of MAPs in strengthening managerial capability and fostering long-term viability. Importantly, behavioral dimensions—particularly founder agency—further condition the adoption and effectiveness of MAPs. Differences in risk preferences, decision styles, and motivational drivers among founders significantly influence the uptake and application of accounting systems. Founders with substantial entrepreneurial capital—including professional experience, technical skills, and social networks—are more inclined to implement sophisticated MAPs (Adjei, 2021; Ahmad et al., 2024; Foris et al., 2022). Hence, behavioral orientation operates as both an enabler and constraint, shaping the institutionalization of accounting practices and the strategic direction of the firm (Krishnan et al., 2022). Despite the explanatory power of contingency theory, the literature has yet to fully conceptualize strategic decision- making as a behavioral mediator within MAP adoption processes. This study addresses that gap by investigating how strategic decisions mediate the relationship between contingency variables and MAP implementation. Specifically, the research examines whether strategic decision-making operationalizes key contextual factors—such as operational technology, environmental uncertainty, organizational culture, and managerial knowledge—into effective accounting practices. In doing so, the study advances contingency theory by integrating behavioral mediation, offering a more comprehensive understanding of how start-ups adopt and internalize MAPs. In addition to providing theoretical contributions, the findings provide actionable insights for practitioners and policy-makers seeking to foster MAP utilization in digital entrepreneurial ecosystems, particularly under conditions of uncertainty and institutional constraints. Therefore, this study aims to examine the mediating role of strategic decision-making in translating key contingency factors—operational technology, environmental uncertainty, organizational culture, and managerial knowledge—into the adoption of management accounting practices among digital start-ups in Indonesia. 2. Methodology This study employs a quantitative, cross-sectional design to investigate the mediating role of strategic decisions in the relationship between contingency factors and the adoption of management accounting practices (MAPs) among digital start- ups. The empirical setting is Palu city, Indonesia, an emerging regional hub for technological entrepreneurship. 2.1. Research Design A quantitative approach was selected to facilitate the empirical examination of latent constructs such as operational technology, environmental uncertainty, organizational culture, managerial knowledge, strategic decisions, and MAPs. Given the exploratory nature of the proposed mediation model and the relatively small sample size, partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) was employed for data analysis. PLS-SEM is particularly suited for theory development and variance-oriented research, enabling simultaneous analysis of complex relationships and tolerance for nonnormal data distributions (Aithal & Aithal, 2020). 2.2. Population and Sampling The study targets founders and senior managers of digital start-ups in Palu city, characterized by early growth stages, technological intensity, and exposure to volatile markets. A purposive sampling method was adopted to recruit respondents actively involved in strategic and financial decision-making. A total of 72 valid responses were obtained through a combination of online and in-person data collection methods. 2.3. Instrumentation Data were gathered via a structured questionnaire comprising multiple items for each variable, measured on a five- point Likert scale ranging from "strongly disagree" to "strongly agree." The constructs were operationalized on the basis of previously validated survey instruments drawn from the extant literature (William, 2024). To enhance content validity and https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Anggraeni et al. (2026) 3 contextual alignment, the instrument underwent expert panel review and was pilot tested with five digital start-ups prior to broader dissemination. 2.4. Validity and Reliability Assessment The construct validity and reliability were evaluated via confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). Internal consistency was established through Cronbach’s alpha and composite reliability, with a threshold of 0.70 serving as the minimum acceptable standard (Branscum, 2020). Convergent validity was assessed via average variance extracted (AVE), whereas discriminant validity was confirmed via the Fornell‒Larcker criterion (Sun et al., 2024). These metrics ensure the theoretical robustness and empirical soundness of the measurement model. 2.5. Data analysis technique PLS‒SEM analysis was conducted via SmartPLS software to test both the structural and measurement models. The bootstrapping procedure, with 5000 resamples, was applied to evaluate the significance of path coefficients and mediation effects. This enabled the identification of both direct and indirect relationships among contingency variables, strategic decisions, and MAP adoption, offering comprehensive insight into the hypothesized behavioral mediation model. 2.6. Ethical Considerations This study did not require formal ethical committee approval as it did not involve any intervention or collection of sensitive personal data. Nevertheless, participation was voluntary and anonymous, and informed consent was obtained from all respondents before completing the questionnaire. 3. Results This chapter presents the empirical findings from the quantitative analysis conducted via partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results are structured into three main subsections: descriptive statistics, path coefficients reflecting direct effects, and mediation analysis. Each finding is interpreted through the lens of existing scholarly literature to ensure both analytical rigor and contextual alignment. 3.1. The data reveal that a majority of founders are young and highly educated, with 73% holding college degrees—consistent with national trends in tech entrepreneurship (Andersson, 2020; Chatra, 2023). The literature suggests that younger entrepreneurs often display greater adaptability to technological change and market volatility (Colombelli & Panelli, 2022). The sampled firms exhibit relatively small-scale operations, characteristic of start-ups in emerging economies (Hasani & O’Reilly, 2021). Table 1 Descriptive Statistics of the Respondents (n = 72). Path Coefficients – Direct Effects The structural model analysis reveals that all four contingency variables—operational technology, environmental uncertainty, organizational culture, and managerial knowledge—significantly and positively influence strategic decision- making. These findings echo the literature on the enabling roles of digital infrastructure, adaptive organizational cultures, and experienced leadership in enhancing decision-making processes and control systems (Khrystenko & Oleksiienko, 2023; Zhang, 2025; Olyfirenko, 2024). Operational technology (β = 0.18, p = 0.041) and environmental uncertainty (β = 0.22, p = 0.028) also contribute significantly, albeit to a lesser extent. Mediation effects Mediation analysis was conducted by bootstrapping procedures in PLS-SEM to assess the indirect effects of contingency factors on MAP adoption via strategic decision-making. The analysis identifies strategic decisions as a significant mediator in the pathways from organizational culture and managerial knowledge to MAP adoption. These results reinforce theoretical perspectives that highlight behavioral and cognitive dimensions as critical to MAP institutionalization (Syahdan et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2025; Yadewani et al., 2023) (Table 3). Mediation Path Indirect Effect p value Organizational Culture → Strategic Decision → MAP 0.13 0.006 Managerial Knowledge → Strategic Decision → MAP 0.15 0.001 Operational Technology → Strategic Decision → MAP 0.08 0.072 Cultural alignment (indirect effect = 0.13, p = 0.006) and managerial competence (indirect effect = 0.15, p = 0.001) demonstrate statistically significant mediation pathways. These findings emphasize the instrumental role of internal cognitive and behavioral capabilities in shaping MAP implementation. Conversely, the mediation effect for operational technology is only marginally significant (indirect effect = 0.08, p = 0.072), suggesting its more limited behavioral transference effect. Overall, the evidence highlights that those behavioral and cognitive enablers—especially those embedded in organizational culture and managerial acumen—exert a more profound effect on MAP adoption than do structural enablers. This aligns with prior research emphasizing the critical role of innovation capacity, leadership dynamics, and access to financial resources in SME accounting practices (Setyawan et al., 2022; Shah et al., 2023). 4. Discussion The results of this study provide compelling evidence that strategic decision-making mediates the effects of both organizational and environmental contingencies on the adoption of Management Accounting Practices (MAPs) in digital start- ups. These findings significantly extend contingency theory by incorporating behavioral dimensions—namely, strategic decisions—as critical mechanisms through which contextual variables are internalized into accounting systems. This behavioral framing moves beyond static fit models and suggests that the alignment between context and practice is actively shaped by the cognitive and interpretive actions of decision-makers (Bui et al., 2023; Nartey et al., 2020). Among the contingency variables examined, organizational culture and managerial knowledge exerted the strongest influence on strategic decision-making. This finding reinforces the growing scholarly consensus that intangible, internal capabilities—particularly those associated with leadership cognition and shared values—serve as fundamental enablers of adaptive strategic behavior. These elements, although frequently underrepresented in structural models, offer the interpretive schemas through which environmental signals are understood and converted into operational responses. The significant mediating role of strategic decisions thus reflects their function as behavioral transmission channels, linking contextual variation with internal accounting system design (Odel, 2022; Wahyuni et al., 2020). From a policy and practice perspective, the findings have critical implications for incubators, accelerators, and entrepreneurship development programs. Efforts to enhance MAP adoption should not only emphasize technical accounting training but also target strategic thinking capabilities. This includes programs that develop founders’ capacity to interpret environmental uncertainty, leverage internal knowledge resources, and make informed, reflective decisions. Tailored mentoring, strategic scenario planning workshops, and the promotion of entrepreneurial reflexivity can foster more robust alignment between strategy and financial management (Ghasemi et al., 2019; Hadianto & Djuminah, 2023). Although the empirical context is limited to digital start-ups in a single regional city in Indonesia, the behavioral mechanisms identified may be applicable—although potentially moderated—in larger or more established firms. In such organizations, strategic decision-making continues to mediate performance outcomes through variables such as organizational culture and leadership style (Owens & McLanahan, 2020; Thomas & Coecke, 2023). However, the bureaucratic rigidity and path dependencies common in mature firms may dampen the agility and immediacy of these behavioral effects. Start-ups, by https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Anggraeni et al. (2026) 5 contrast, due to their flatter structures and resource constraints, are more likely to exhibit pronounced behavioral mediation, where cognitive alignment and cultural adaptability play outsized roles (Zahed et al., 2022). Despite the study’s contributions, notable theoretical and empirical gaps remain. In particular, individual-level behavioral traits—such as founders’ risk tolerance, motivation, or cognitive biases—have yet to be systematically integrated into accounting adoption frameworks. Future research should explore how these microlevel variables interact with the organizational context to shape accounting system outcomes. Moreover, cross-regional studies could illuminate how institutional environments and cultural dimensions moderate the effectiveness of behavioral mediation mechanisms (Ammerman et al., 2025; Han et al., 2019; Untarini, 2020). Integrating psychological and behavioral constructs into contingency-based accounting models offers a promising pathway toward a more holistic understanding of MAP implementation. In conclusion, the incorporation of strategic decision-making as a behavioral mediator within contingency theory provides a nuanced and dynamic perspective on MAP adoption in digital start-ups. Rather than being driven solely by structural or environmental alignment, effective accounting system implementation depends on the cognitive capabilities and strategic orientations of key decision-makers. This behavioral extension not only deepens theoretical insight but also offers practical strategies for building adaptive, contextually responsive financial infrastructures in emerging entrepreneurial ecosystems. 5. Limitations and Future Lines of Research This study is not without limitations. First, the conceptual framework focuses primarily on digital start-ups, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to more established firms or nondigital industries. The dynamic and uncertain environment of start-ups, particularly in the digital sector, may produce unique behavioral patterns in strategic decision- making that differ from those of traditional businesses. Second, the study places strategic decision-making as the central mediating variable, whereas other behavioral or organizational constructs—such as leadership style, organizational culture, or learning orientation—may also play significant roles in shaping the relationship between contingency factors and management accounting practices. Third, methodological constraints such as reliance on cross-sectional data or self-reported measures could introduce bias, making it difficult to fully capture the dynamic interplay of contingency factors, decision-making behavior, and accounting practices over time. Finally, the cultural and institutional context in which digital start-ups operate may also influence outcomes, meaning that findings might vary across regions, countries, or regulatory environments. Future research can address these limitations in several ways. First, comparative studies between digital start-ups and more mature organizations could provide insights into whether the mediating role of strategic decision-making is unique to high-growth, uncertain environments or applicable more broadly. Second, future scholars may incorporate additional mediating or moderating variables such as leadership dynamics, innovation capability, or organizational resilience to better explain behavioral mechanisms. Third, adopting longitudinal or mixed-method approaches would allow for a deeper understanding of how contingency factors and decision-making behaviors evolve and shape management accounting practices over time. Fourth, cross-cultural or cross-industry studies could enhance the external validity of the framework by exploring how institutional settings, cultural norms, and regulatory structures affect the proposed relationships. Finally, future research might integrate digital transformation elements, such as the role of big data analytics and AI-driven decision support systems, to explore how technology interacts with behavioral decision-making processes in influencing management accounting practices. 6. Conclusions The findings of this study affirm that strategic decision-making serves as a significant mediating mechanism linking organizational culture and managerial knowledge to the adoption of management accounting practices (MAPs) in digital start- ups. While operational technology and environmental uncertainty influence decision-making directly, their indirect effects on MAP implementation were found to be limited. This evidence underscores that MAP adoption is not solely contingent upon structural or environmental alignment but is strongly driven by the behavioral capacity of decision-makers. The integration of strategic decision-making into the contingency theory framework offers a more nuanced understanding of how context-specific variables are cognitively interpreted and operationalized into accounting practices. From a theoretical perspective, this research contributes to the advancement of contingency-based accounting scholarship by foregrounding behavioral mediation as a critical explanatory pathway. Strategic decision-making is positioned here as a core behavioral construct that translates external complexity and internal dynamics into concrete accounting actions. Future research should deepen this behavioral orientation by investigating the roles of cognitive flexibility, leadership styles, and individual entrepreneurial traits across various institutional and cultural contexts. In terms of policy and practice, the findings suggest that incubators and entrepreneurial support programs should extend beyond technical training to emphasize the cognitive and strategic competencies of founders. (2026) 6 interventions—such as reflective leadership mentoring, scenario-based decision-making modules, and experiential financial simulations—could significantly strengthen the behavioral foundations necessary for effective MAP adoption. In conclusion, strategic decision-making emerges as a vital behavioral link in the contingency-based implementation of MAPs. Its central role in translating contextual pressures into accounting practices highlights the imperative for both cognitive development and organizational learning in fostering resilient and adaptive financial systems within digital entrepreneurial environments. JSON: Name: strategic_decision_mediation_map Title: Quantitative mediation analysis using PLS-SEM of how strategic decision-making transmits contingency factors to management accounting practice adoption in digital start-ups Short Hypothesis: Strategic decision-making mediates the positive effects of organizational culture and managerial knowledge on the level of management accounting practice adoption in digital start-ups. Related Work: Prior work applies contingency theory to explain MAP adoption by linking structural and environmental contingencies (operational technology, environmental uncertainty, culture, managerial knowledge) to accounting system design, typically using cross-sectional survey designs and variance-based SEM. Existing approaches emphasize direct alignment between context and accounting tools or examine single antecedents in isolation. Limitations include heavy reliance on direct-effect models that omit behavioral mediation, frequent use of small regional samples that reduce external validity, predominance of self-reported cross-sectional data that limit causal inference, inconsistent construct validation practices across studies, and sparse comparisons between variance-based and covariance-based SEM results. Additionally, prior studies rarely test alternative mediators (e.g., leadership style, learning orientation) or conduct ablation/robustness checks (multi-group, alternative estimators), leaving unresolved whether managerial cognition (strategic decision-making) is the operative transmission mechanism. Abstract: This research tests whether strategic decision-making functions as a behavioral mediator that transmits contingency factors (operational technology, environmental uncertainty, organizational culture, managerial knowledge) into the adoption of management accounting practices among digital start-ups. The approach uses a quantitative mediation framework implemented with partial least squares structural equation modeling to estimate measurement and structural parameters and to evaluate indirect effects. The main contribution is the formal identification and empirical testing of strategic decision-making as the behavioral bridge between contextual contingencies and accounting practice adoption, extending contingency theory by incorporating managerial cognition into the causal chain. Expected outcomes include quantification of direct and indirect path coefficients, variance explained in strategic decision-making and MAP adoption, and comparative evidence on model robustness versus alternative mediators and estimation methods. Results will inform theory by clarifying behavioral transmission mechanisms and provide empirically grounded priorities for training and incubation programs that seek to increase MAP uptake in entrepreneurial ecosystems. Experiments: Datasets: Primary cross-sectional survey of digital start-ups founders/financial managers across three Indonesian metropolitan regions; target N = 220 valid responses; inclusion: digital product/service start-ups, operational <=10 years, respondent in strategic/financial role. Measurement: multi-item reflective scales for operational technology (OT), environmental uncertainty (EU), organizational culture (OC), managerial knowledge (MK), strategic decision-making (SDM), and management accounting practices (MAP); 5-point Likert. Baselines: (A) direct-effects model (contingency factors → MAP) without SDM; (B) full mediation model (contingency → SDM → MAP); (C) alternative-mediator models replacing SDM with leadership style and with learning orientation; (D) covariance-based SEM (CB-SEM) implementation for robustness. Evaluation metrics: measurement model – Cronbach's alpha, composite reliability (CR>0.70), AVE (>0.50), item loadings (>0.70), HTMT (<0.90), VIF (<5); structural model – path coefficients with bootstrap t-statistics and p-values, R2, Q2 (predictive relevance), f2 effect sizes, SRMR, and indirect effect confidence intervals (bias-corrected bootstrap, 5000 resamples). Experimental setup: run PLS-SEM (software: SmartPLS or equivalent) with 5000 bootstrap resamples; report standardized path coefficients and 95% bootstrap CIs; perform nested model comparison (A vs B) via changes in R2 and SRMR and significance of indirect paths; perform ablation study by sequentially removing SDM and comparing MAP R2 and direct path significance; conduct multi-group analysis by region and start-up age (<=3 years vs >3 years) to test invariance; implement CB-SEM on same data to compare coefficient signs, magnitudes, and fit indices (CFI, TLI, RMSEA). Risk Factors and Limitations: Cross-sectional survey design limits causal inference and temporal ordering of mediation; self-reported measures introduce common-method variance and social desirability bias; sample bias from regional concentration reduces external generalizability to other countries or larger firms; modest sample size may reduce power to detect small indirect effects and interactions; measurement model misspecification (poorly fitting items) can invalidate structural conclusions; collinearity among contingency predictors may inflate standard errors and bias effect-size estimates; PLS-SEM reliance on approximate fit and distribution-free assumptions can yield different conclusions than CB-SEM in presence of model misspecification; omitted variable bias (unmeasured individual traits or firm resources) may confound mediator estimates; potential reciprocal causation between SDM and MAP (simultaneity) undermines strict mediation interpretation; nonresponse and missing data patterns may bias estimates if not missing completely at random; findings may not scale to mature firms or non-digital industries.
